catalog_quote: 140. Stress and Intonation With minor exceptions, words and phrases in isolation have one major stress on the penultimate syllable. This primary stress /’/ is accompanied by a rise in the pitch of the syllable bearing it to level 3. Although nearly all words in isolation have penultimate stress, this stress may be lost ... or shifted to meet the conditions of penultimate phrasal stress. Phrases are marked by certain juncture features as well as the noticeable stress placement and can consist ... One class of exceptions to penultimate stress are three-syllable A-induced noun plurals (see 430). In these words the stress is on the antepenult.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Kroeber (Yaudanchi, 1907): word stress is weak; a long vowel in any of the last three syllables carries the accent; words with no long vowel are stressed on the penult (sometimes antepenult); the 'normal accent' rests on the penult. Suffixation and reduplication move the accent. NOTE: the later and modern sources reached at search-snippet evidence give plain penultimate stress: Newman 1944 sect. 4:1 'Words are regularly accented on the penult' (six dialects incl. Yawdanchi and Wikchamni) and Gamble 1978 sect. 140 'With minor exceptions, words and phrases in isolation have one major stress on the penultimate syllable' (Wikchamni); Kroeber 1963: 182 himself concedes stress 'falls so regularly on the penult' and that he tended to write spurious length in stressed syllables, so his 1907 long-vowel-attracts-accent statement is best read as impressionistic. If the catalog prefers the modern primaries, the reading for tule1245 is fixed: penultimate syllable.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Kroeber 1907 says nothing about secondary stress. Gamble 1978 snippet: 'This primary stress /'/ is accompanied by a..' (continuation not recovered; probably pitch/intonation).
new_statements.exceptions: Kroeber 1907: 'a few exceptions such as pa′t·ūjac' (long vowel not accented); enclitic pronouns/particles am, hin, hi are accentless and draw the accent of the preceding word; plural suffixes move the accent forward or backward, objective suffixes do not (p. 200). Newman 1944: exceptions to penult in words whose final syllable contains durative -xo· (and further classes not recovered). Gamble 1978: three-syllable A-induced noun plurals have antepenultimate stress; Kroeber 1963: 226 antepenult stress frequent in plurals of tribal names.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level ('separate words', 'isolated word'), but Kroeber notes that in connected speech the word accent 'tends to disappear.. as against the accent of the phrase or sentence' and that enclitic groups carry one accent; Gamble 1978 likewise states that penultimate word stress may be lost or shifted under penultimate phrasal stress. Kroeber 1907: 255 admits word accent was not specially attended to when recording the texts.
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted statement describes the Yaudanchi (Yawdanchi) dialect, Glottolog yawd1234, one of the two dialects Glottolog places under tule1245 (the other is Wikchamni/Wukchumni wikc1234). Gamble 1978 and Newman 1944 (search-snippet evidence) describe Wikchamni (and, for Newman, also Yawdanchi) with plain penultimate stress. Caution on duplication: per the earlier catalog verification held by the project), the catalog already holds a 'Wikchamni' record (an earlier reading, the StressTyp2 entry for this language < Gamble 1978 sect. 140, fixed penult) keyed to yoku1256 / ISO yok ('Northern Yokuts'), although the language it describes is a tule1245 dialect; a tule1245 record built from Kroeber 1907 would be a second record for the same Glottolog language unless that record is re-keyed.

readall_conflicts: No disagreement on placement: Kroeber 1907 (Yaudanchi; the existing statement), Gamble 1978 (Wikchamni) and Newman 1944 (six dialects incl. Wikchamni and Yawdanchi) all put word stress on the penult. They differ on how marked stress is and on the exception classes: Kroeber says word accent is 'not very marked' and 'partly dependent on quantity of vowels' (a long vowel in the last three syllables carries the accent; otherwise penult, sometimes antepenult), whereas Newman calls stress 'well marked' and 'mechanical' with morphological exceptions (durative -xo· final syllables) and Gamble states penultimate stress with an antepenult exception in three-syllable A-induced noun plurals plus phrase-level shifts. Kroeber 1963 (held by the project in the sibling yoku1256 folder) himself attributes his 1906-07 non-penult stresses partly to informant deviation on isolated words, so the quantity-sensitivity in Kroeber 1907 is best carried as a hedged early-source note, not as a competing rule.org 401/403; Newman: HathiTrust not reachable by automated download, two attempts each); both readings rest on Open Library full-text-search snippets saved held by the project.

sources.note: A short (6 pp.) loanword-adaptation study; likely to show how Spanish stress and segments are nativised into Wikchamni (penultimate stress, vowel length); no lexical tone content expected since Yokuts is described without tone (Gamble 1978 sect. 140 treats pitch rise as a correlate of stress). Listed as a Wikchamni-specific phonology-adjacent article not previously listed here, not as a tone description.
